title: The Wardrobe of the fourth floor walk-up
premise: Oscar Joubert, once the conservatory's most celebrated piano prodigy before a public breakdown ended his career, returns years later as a janitor, hiding behind practiced smiles and a mop. When his estranged mother dies, a stranger named Vivienne appears at the funeral calling the family by a name no one has used in decades, claiming to be the daughter Oscar's father abandoned and Oscar's secret half-sister. As they sort the house for sale, Oscar discovers his father was not merely unfaithful but had traded Oscar's conservatory future to protect his own reputation, a corruption of power that shaped Oscar's entire fall. To stop the sale of the house, Oscar and Vivienne must reconcile with the versions of themselves in the old photographs; the novel ends with Oscar withdrawing the house from the market, giving Vivienne the ground floor, and returning to the conservatory not as a janitor or a prodigy, but as a teacher of the students everyone else has given up on.
about_author: P. M. Delacroix is the pen name of a former conservatory archivist who spent fifteen years cataloguing the letters of musicians who never became famous. They live above a closed piano shop in Lyon and write only in the early morning, before the street sweepers arrive.

chapters.title: The Smile That Ends Conversations
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. We follow a day in his janitorial life at the conservatory, past practice rooms where his old name is still engraved on a plaque he dusts but never reads. A young failing student, Marguerite, asks him if he ever played. His smile ends the conversation, but he lingers by her door after she leaves. Emotional beat: the cost of invisibility chosen daily.

chapters.title: A Name Nobody Uses
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. At his mother's sparse funeral, a composed stranger in a grey coat approaches the family plot and calls the Jouberts by the name 'Aubry'—a name Oscar hasn't heard since childhood. She introduces herself as Vivienne and says she has a right to be here. His brother Étienne demands she leave. Emotional beat: the past arriving uninvited, refusing to stay buried.

chapters.title: Fourth Floor, No Elevator
chapters.summary: Vivienne's POV. She explains her claim: their father, Marcel, had another family for nine years. She shows Oscar a photograph of Marcel holding a baby in front of the walk-up. Oscar recognizes his father's watch, his mother's curtains. He says nothing, but that night he doesn't sleep. Emotional beat: the vertigo of discovering a second version of your own childhood.

chapters.title: The Inventory
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. Forced by the estate lawyer to sort the house together before sale, Oscar and Vivienne work in hostile silence, dividing objects into keep, sell, discard. They find a locked cedar wardrobe on the fourth floor that neither has the key to, which the sale contract oddly excludes. Emotional beat: grief performed as bureaucracy, resentment sharpening into curiosity.

chapters.title: Marguerite's Hands
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Back at the conservatory, Marguerite practices the same Chopin nocturne Oscar performed at his debut. He corrects her fingering before he can stop himself. Her teacher notices, and the conservatory director, who remembers Oscar's scandal, begins watching him. Emotional beat: the dangerous warmth of being needed again.

chapters.title: What Marcel Traded
chapters.summary: Vivienne's POV. Vivienne finds correspondence hidden in her mother's effects: letters showing Marcel paid the conservatory director to guarantee Oscar's career in exchange for burying a plagiarism accusation—against Marcel himself. Oscar's prodigy status was purchased, and the director has held this over the family for thirty years. Emotional beat: love curdling into the realization that duty was a leash.

chapters.title: The Key in the Piano Bench
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Oscar finds the wardrobe key inside his mother's piano bench, wrapped in the program from his debut. Inside the wardrobe: his father's real compositions, brilliant and uncredited, published under the director's name. Oscar understands his breakdown, his father's silence, his mother's coldness—everything was protection. Emotional beat: fury and grief arriving together.

chapters.title: The Director's Offer
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. The director confronts Oscar: sign away the wardrobe's contents and the family name, and Marguerite gets a solo; refuse, and Oscar's old scandal is revived. Étienne, desperate for the sale money, sides with the director. Vivienne, however, chooses Oscar. Emotional beat: the corruption of power demanding its price, and the first real act of family.

chapters.title: Everything in the Wardrobe
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Climax. At the conservatory's winter recital, Oscar takes the stage uninvited, plays his father's unpublished work from memory, and tells the room whose music it is. The director's reputation collapses; the sale of the house, contingent on the wardrobe's exclusion, is voided. Emotional beat: the prodigy returns, not to reclaim glory but to give a dead man his name back.

chapters.title: Ground Floor, Garden Side
chapters.summary: Vivienne's POV, closing with Oscar's. Spring. Oscar withdraws the house from sale, keeps the fourth floor, and signs the ground floor over to Vivienne. He begins teaching Marguerite and students like her—unpolished, overlooked. In the last scene, he hangs a restored photograph of both families, Aubry and Joubert, in the stairwell where everyone must pass it. Emotional beat: forgiveness as a structural renovation, not a feeling.
